title: The Life of St. Mary of Egypt
subtitle: Selections from the Life by St. Sophronius of Jerusalem
source: Summarized from public-domain English renderings of the Greek Life. Marginal notes by the editors of Purify.

sections.title: Stopped at the door of the Sepulchre
paragraphs: Sophronius tells the story as it was told to him by the priest Zosimas. Mary had crossed the sea with a band of pilgrims, paying her passage with her body all along the way, and joined the crowd in Jerusalem flooding the Church of the Resurrection on the feast of the Holy Cross. She tried to enter with the rest, and could not. Three times she pressed forward; three times an unseen force held her back at the door.

She withdrew to the courtyard and saw an icon of the Theotokos. There, suddenly, she understood that her body had become unfit to come near the Cross, and that the woman in the icon was nearer to God than any priest. She prayed there, weeping, promising to leave her old life if she might only be permitted to venerate the wood on which her Lord had been crucified.

She tried the door again, and now the crowd parted before her. She venerated the Cross, returned to the icon, and asked what she should do next. She heard within her heart the answer: 'Cross the Jordan, and there you will find rest.' The same day she bought three small loaves with the only money she had not spent on sin, and walked out into the desert. She did not return for forty-seven years.
notes: Mary's first failed approach to the Sepulchre is a parable the Fathers love. The doors of the Church are open to sinners, but they are not open to sin. The shift in her happens at the icon of the Theotokos, who is herself the door without sin through whom God came among us.
Sophronius wrote the Life around 638 while Patriarch of Jerusalem. He had heard the story from monks of the Jordan, who had heard it from the brothers of Zosimas's monastery.

sections.title: Communion by the Jordan
paragraphs: Zosimas had retreated into the same desert for the great fast of Lent, as the rule of his community required. Far from any path he saw at a distance a figure with sun-blackened skin and hair white as snow. He ran toward it; it ran from him; he called out asking it to wait and to receive his prayers. The figure asked him first to throw down his cloak so that she might cover her nakedness.

She told him her name and her story, and she made him promise to tell no one until she had died. The next year, she said, on Great Thursday, he was to bring the Holy Mysteries to the bank of the Jordan, and she would meet him there. The year passed. On the night of the Mystical Supper Zosimas waited by the river, and Mary appeared, walking across the water. She received Communion from him with bitter weeping, asked him to come again the following year, and disappeared into the dark.

When he returned the year after he found her dead, her body undecayed, her arms folded in prayer over her heart. Beside her was scratched in the sand the date of her repose and the request that her body be buried. The desert lion that approached helped him dig the grave.
notes: The reading of the Life in monastic services on the Thursday of the fifth week of Great Lent is paired with the chanting of the Great Canon of St. Andrew of Crete, the longest penitential text in the Orthodox tradition.
Orthodox tradition does not make a cult of Mary's sins; it points to the strength of the Sacraments that wrought her transfiguration over forty-seven years in a place no one saw.
